# Arrays


<!-- WARNING: THIS FILE WAS AUTOGENERATED! DO NOT EDIT! -->

BPL has two kinds of value. Numbers, characters and functions are atoms.
An array is a rectangular collection of values, including other arrays.
This is the *based array* model, named in a [1981
paper](https://dl.acm.org/doi/abs/10.1145/586656.586663) and popularized
by [BQN](https://mlochbaum.github.io/BQN/doc/based.html).

## Writing vectors

Write a vector by putting its items in brackets, separated by spaces. An
item can be any expression without a space in it, such as a number, a
name, `≥x` or a string:

``` bpl
x←10
[x ≥x "hi"]
```

    10 11 "hi"

A bracket list is a vector, however many items it has.
[`ρ`](https://answerdotai.github.io/basedpl/glyphs/rho.html) shows that
`[5]` has one axis of length 1, whereas the number `5` has no axes:

``` bpl
ρ[5]
ρ5
```

    [1]ₓ

    ⍬ₓ

You can omit the brackets around a list of literals. Values written side
by side form a [strand](terms.qmd#term-strand), the same vector as the
bracket list:

``` bpl
1 2 3≡[1 2 3]
```

    $t

Names side by side form a strand too:

``` bpl
a←1
b←2
a b
```

    1 2

Matrices are written in brackets too, one row per line. [Types of
brackets](bracket-types.ipynb) covers this array notation, along with
what `;` and
[`◇`](https://answerdotai.github.io/basedpl/glyphs/diamond.html) mean
inside brackets:

``` bpl
m←[1 2 3
   4 5 6]
m
```

    1 2 3
    4 5 6

## Shape and rank

An array’s shape lists the lengths of its axes. Its rank is the number
of axes, the tally of its shape. Scalars, vectors and matrices are the
arrays of rank 0, 1 and 2. `m` has two rows and three columns:

``` bpl
ρm
≢ρm
```

    [2 3]ₓ

    2ₓ

[`ρ`](https://answerdotai.github.io/basedpl/glyphs/rho.html) builds an
array of any shape from the items on its right. `ι6` counts from 0 to 5:

``` bpl
2 3ρι6ₓ
```

    [0 1 2
     3 4 5]ₓ

An axis can have length 0. This matrix has no rows and three columns:

``` bpl
ρ0 3ρ0
```

    [0 3]ₓ

[`,`](https://answerdotai.github.io/basedpl/glyphs/comma.html) lists the
items in row-major order:

``` bpl
,m
```

    1 2 3 4 5 6

## Atoms and scalars

An atom has no axes, and neither does a scalar, which is the array of
rank 0. Enclose
[`⊂`](https://answerdotai.github.io/basedpl/glyphs/left-shoe.html) gives
a scalar holding its argument:

``` bpl
ρ3
ρ⊂3
```

    ⍬ₓ

    ⍬ₓ

`3` and `⊂3` are still different values. The scalar `⊂3` is an array
with one position, holding the atom `3`:

``` bpl
3≡⊂3
```

    $f

Enclosing always adds a layer, even around an atom.
[`≡`](https://answerdotai.github.io/basedpl/glyphs/equal-underbar.html)
counts the layers:

``` bpl
≡3
≡⊂3
≡⊂⊂3
```

    0ₓ

    1ₓ

    2ₓ

[`⊂`](https://answerdotai.github.io/basedpl/glyphs/left-shoe.html)
encloses only [subjects](terms.qmd#term-subject). For a function `f`,
the scalar holding it is `fˢ`:

``` bpl
≡+ˢ
```

    1ₓ

## Nesting

The items of an array can be arrays. This vector holds two vectors of
different lengths:

``` bpl
n←[[1 2] [3 4 5]]
n
```

    (1 2◇3 4 5)

[`↑`](https://answerdotai.github.io/basedpl/glyphs/up-arrow.html) gives
the first item. Each
[`¨`](https://answerdotai.github.io/basedpl/glyphs/diaeresis.html)
applies a function to every item, here Tally
[`≢`](https://answerdotai.github.io/basedpl/glyphs/equal-underbar-slash.html):

``` bpl
↑n
≢¨n
```

    1 2

    [2 3]ₓ

`n`, a vector of vectors of numbers, has depth 2:

``` bpl
≡n
```

    2ₓ

Arithmetic, Each and indexing on a scalar give a scalar, not the atom
inside it:

``` bpl
⊂3 + 4
-¨⊂3
```

    ⊂7

    ⊂¯3

Rank and the search functions work on whole cells instead, as
[Rank](glyphs/jot-diaeresis.qmd) describes.

## Fill

Every array has a [prototype](terms.qmd#term-prototype), the value that
it supplies as fill: zero for numbers, a space for characters, and a
filled copy of the first item for nested arrays.
[`↑`](https://answerdotai.github.io/basedpl/glyphs/up-arrow.html) pads
with fill when its left argument is greater than the length of its right
argument:

``` bpl
5↑[1 2]
"<",3↑"ab" , ">"
```

    1 2 0 0 0

    "<ab >"

An empty array keeps its prototype. First of `0ρn` gives the fill of
`1 2`, the first item of `n`:

``` bpl
↑0ρn
```

    0 0

When results of different lengths are assembled into one array, the
shorter ones are padded with fill. `≥ι` counts from 1 up to its
argument, and with `⁰` it runs once for each item, which gives one row
per count:

``` bpl
≥ι ⁰ [2 4]
```

    1 2 0 0
    1 2 3 4

Each keeps the results as separate items instead:

``` bpl
≥ι ¨[2 4]
```

    (1 2◇1 2 3 4)

## Keys

Keys label the positions along an axis. Write them with
[`:`](https://answerdotai.github.io/basedpl/glyphs/colon.html), then
pick an item by its key with a dot:

``` bpl
T←"x" "y":1 2
T
T.x
```

    ["x":1 "y":2]

    1

Axes can also have names. Pass Reshape a keyed shape to name the axes it
builds. [Axis keys](keyed.ipynb) covers keyed arrays in full:

``` bpl
M←["city":2 "month":3]ρι6ₓ
ρM
```

    ["city":2 "month":3]ₓ

## Functions in arrays

An array can hold functions. `fs` is a vector of three functions:

``` bpl
fs←[+ × ÷]
fs
```

    [+ × ÷]

Selecting an item gives back a function. A
[subscript](scripts.ipynb#subscripts) selects one position. To call the
selected function, name it first, as with any function that a call or a
selection returns:

``` bpl
times←fs₁
2 times 3
```

    6

Pick
[`⊃`](https://answerdotai.github.io/basedpl/glyphs/right-shoe.html),
First [`↑`](https://answerdotai.github.io/basedpl/glyphs/up-arrow.html)
and [Index](glyphs/squad.qmd)
[`⌷`](https://answerdotai.github.io/basedpl/glyphs/squad.html) with a
single position also return stored functions. `↑⌽fs` is the last
function in `fs`:

``` bpl
div←↑⌽fs
6 div 3
```

    2

A list can mix functions with other values, including a vector of
functions as one item:

``` bpl
mixed←[[1 2 3] + ×]
≢mixed
≢[fs ÷]
```

    3ₓ

    2ₓ

Successive Picks select items from successively nested arrays. Picking
with an empty vector returns the right argument unchanged:

``` bpl
x←[[+ ×] [- ÷]]
f←1⊃0⊃x
2 f 3
⍬⊃n ≡ n
```

    6

    $t

A dfn can return a function it selects.
[Agenda](glyphs/diamond-underbar.qmd) selects one and calls it in one
step:

``` bpl
g←{1⊃ω}fs
2 g 3
```

    6

An array that holds a function as an item is callable. Each function is
called with the whole arguments, and each other item is returned
unchanged:

``` bpl
2 fs 8
```

    10 16 0.25

The results have the array’s shape and keys as their frame, as
[Rank](glyphs/jot-diaeresis.qmd)’s results do. Calling a keyed array of
aggregation functions gives a keyed result, and calling it through Rank
gives one row of results for each row of its argument. Write Rank out as
`⍤1` here, because `stats¹` would raise the items of `stats` to a power:

``` bpl
stats←["mean":+/÷≢ "max":⌈/]
stats 3 1 4 1 5
stats⍤1[3 1 4◇1 5 9]
```

    ["mean":2.8 "max":5]

           mean max
    2.666666667   4
              5   9

Results of different shapes are padded with fill:

``` bpl
[ι ⊢] 3
```

    0 1 2
    3 0 0

An array is callable only when one of its direct items is a function.
Calling a scalar that holds a function, such as `-ˢ`, calls that
function, and its empty frame adds no axis. An enclosed function array
holds an array rather than a function, so `(⊂fs) 2` is a strand:

``` bpl
-ˢ 3
(⊂fs) 2
```

    ¯3

    [⊂[+ × ÷] 2]

A function array acts as a function only where a subject follows it.
Elsewhere it’s an array, so `≢fs` counts its items.
[Binding](evaluation.qmd#binding) gives the rule, and [Operators and
operands](evaluation.qmd#operators-and-operands) says which operators
call the array:

``` bpl
≢fs
```

    3ₓ

An array holds a function item as a reference to the function. Reshape,
selection, catenation and the other structural functions move function
items without running them. Display prints each function as its source.
A native function with no source spelling, such as a generator’s `roll`,
prints in `⟨…⟩`. A function’s fill is the function itself:

``` bpl
5↑fs
```

    [+ × ÷ + +]

Two functions match when they’re built from matching parts. A primitive
matches itself, as does a derived function such as `+/`, however many
times either is written. A dfn matches only itself. Two separately
written `{ω}` don’t match, even though they do the same thing. Functions
have no ordering, and Grade and Interval Index reject them.

``` bpl
[+]≡[+]
[+/]≡[+/]
h←{ω}
[h]≡[h]
[{ω}]≡[{ω}]
```

    $t

    $t

    $t

    $f

A dfn can return a function. A function that a dfn defines in its body
works only while the call that defined it is running. Returning such a
function, or storing it anywhere that outlives the call, including
inside an array or an empty array’s prototype, raises a `DOMAIN` error.

In Python, arrays of functions work as [Callable
functions](python.ipynb#callable-functions) describes.
